    Unit 1.1

    Negative numbers & place value

    Theory

    1Place value in big numbers

    In a number with many digits, every digit sits in a place, and that place tells you the digit's value. In 45 672: the digit 4 is in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 40 000 — but the digit 2 is in the ones place, so it is only worth 2. We write big numbers in groups of 3 digits to make them easy to read: 45 672 is read as “forty-five thousand, six hundred and seventy-two”.

    Place value chart — the bottom line is the expanded form of the number.

    2Negative numbers and the number line

    Numbers do not stop at zero! Negative numbers are numbers less than 0, written with a minus sign in front, like −3. On the number line, negative numbers sit to the left of zero. The further left you go, the smaller the number; the further right, the bigger. So −7 is smaller than −2, and every negative number is smaller than 0.

    Hà Nội: 25°C

    25 degrees ABOVE zero — a positive number

    Sa Pa (frosty night): −3°C

    3 degrees BELOW zero — a negative number. Colder than 0°C!

    3Counting through zero

    When you count back, do not stop at 0 — keep going into the negative numbers: 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3… Watch out: the number right after 0 when counting back is −1 (not −0!). On the number line, every step back is a hop to the left, and every step forward is a hop to the right.

    3 − 7 = −4: start at 3, hop back 7 steps, straight through zero, and land on −4.

    4Comparing numbers: <, > and =

    We compare two numbers with the symbols: > (greater than), < (less than) and = (equal to). Memory trick: the wide-open mouth always “eats” the bigger number! For two numbers with the same number of digits, compare digit by digit from the left — the first place where they differ decides which number is bigger.

    Positive vs negativeAny positive number beats any negative number: 1 > −100!
    Two negativesThe one closer to zero is bigger: −2 > −7.
    More digitsFor positive numbers: more digits means bigger: 10 234 > 9 876.

    5Ordering numbers

    Ascending order means smallest to largest; descending order means largest to smallest. The best strategy: picture (or sketch) the numbers on a number line — then just read them off from left to right for ascending order. Remember: negative numbers always come before 0, and −8 comes before −3!

    Put all 5 numbers on the number line, then read left to right → ascending. Read right to left → descending.

    6Rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1 000

    To round a number means to snap it to the nearest “friendly” number — the nearest ten, hundred or thousand. The method: look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If that digit is 0–4 → round down; if it is 5–9 → round up. On a number line, the rounded number is simply the nearest landmark — and if you are exactly halfway, the rule says go up.

    Next digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4Round DOWN — the place digit stays the same. 3 429 → 3 400 (nearest 100).
    Next digit is 5, 6, 7, 8, 9Round UP — the place digit goes up by one. 3 471 → 3 500 (nearest 100).
    NumberNearest 10Nearest 100Nearest 1 000
    3 4713 4703 5003 000
    68 51968 52068 50069 000
    45 50045 50045 50046 000 (halfway → up)

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    At night in Sa Pa, the temperature is −6°C. By midday, the temperature has risen by 9 degrees. What is the midday temperature?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Start at −6 on the number line.
    2. The temperature rising means hopping 9 steps to the right.
    3. From −6, it takes 6 steps just to reach 0. That leaves 9 − 6 = 3 more steps on the positive side.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 3°C. From −6, go up 6 degrees to reach 0, then 3 more: −6 + 9 = 3.
    Example 2

    Put these numbers in ascending order: 2 305, 2 350, 2 035, −5, 0.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The negative number is always smallest → −5 goes first. 0 comes right after it.
    2. The other three all have 4 digits and start with 2 — compare the hundreds digit: 2 035, 2 305, 2 350.
    3. 2 035 has 0 hundreds → smallest of the three. For the last two, compare the tens: 2 305 < 2 350.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: −5, 0, 2 035, 2 305, 2 350.
    Example 3

    Round 47 638 to the nearest 10, the nearest 100, and the nearest 1 000.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Nearest 10: look at the ones digit — 47638. 8 ≥ 5 → the tens go up: 47 640.
    2. Nearest 100: look at the tens digit — 47638. 3 ≤ 4 → the hundreds stay: 47 600.
    3. Nearest 1 000: look at the hundreds digit — 47638. 6 ≥ 5 → the thousands go up: 48 000.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 47 640 (nearest 10) · 47 600 (nearest 100) · 48 000 (nearest 1 000). Same number, three different answers — because each time we aim at a different place!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Tenths and hundredths

    The place value chart does not stop at the ones! After the decimal point, the places keep getting smaller: the tenths place, then the hundredths place. In 3.47: there are 3 ones, 4 tenths (0.4) and 7 hundredths (0.07). Each place is worth 1/10 of the place to its left.

    The black dot is the decimal point — the border between the whole part and the parts smaller than 1.

    2Decimals on the number line

    Between two neighbouring whole numbers lives a whole “world” of decimals! Split the gap from 3 to 4 into 10 equal parts, and each mark is one tenth: 3.1, 3.2, 3.3… The number 3.5 sits exactly in the middle. To find 3.47, split the gap between 3.4 and 3.5 into 10 hundredths again.

    3Adding and subtracting: line up the points

    The golden rule: line up the decimal points, so tenths add to tenths and ones add to ones. If one number is shorter, pad it with a zero (2.7 = 2.70). Then add or subtract in columns as usual — and don't forget to estimate first, to check your answer is sensible!

    4Multiplying and dividing by 10 and 100: digits slide

    Multiplying by 10 makes every digit slide one place to the left (the number becomes 10 times bigger); dividing by 10 makes them slide one place to the right. For 100, slide two places. Note: it is the digits that move — the decimal point always stays still!

    × 10, × 100Digits slide LEFT 1 place (×10) or 2 places (×100): 2.5 × 10 = 25; 0.34 × 100 = 34.
    ÷ 10, ÷ 100Digits slide RIGHT 1 place (÷10) or 2 places (÷100): 74 ÷ 10 = 7.4; 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5.

    5Multiplying and dividing decimals by whole numbers

    Multiplying a decimal by a whole number is just repeated addition: 2.4 × 3 = 2.4 + 2.4 + 2.4 = 7.2. Dividing is the reverse — sharing into equal parts: 7.2 ÷ 3 = 2.4. Checking trick: a multiplication answer should be bigger, and a division answer smaller, than the number you started with (when multiplying/dividing by a number bigger than 1).

    2.4 + 2.4 + 2.4
    2.4 × 3 = 7.2
    7.2 ÷ 3 = 2.4 (share into 3)

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna buys a book for $4.83 and a pen for $2.90. How much does she spend in total?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Estimate first: $4.83 is near $5, $2.90 is near $3 → the answer should be near $8.
    2. Line up the decimal points: 4.83 + 2.90.
    3. Add column by column from the right: 3+0=3 (hundredths); 8+9=17 → write 7, carry 1; 4+2+1=7.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: $7.73 — nicely close to the $8 estimate, so we can trust it.
    Example 2

    Work these out quickly: 6.3 × 10, 6.3 × 100, and 630 ÷ 100.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. × 10: digits slide 1 place left → 63.
    2. × 100: slide 2 places left → 630.
    3. ÷ 100: slide 2 places right → 6.3 — exactly where we started, because ×100 then ÷100 brings you home!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 6.3 × 10 = 63 · 6.3 × 100 = 630 · 630 ÷ 100 = 6.3.
    Example 3

    Three friends share 7.2 kg of oranges equally. How many kilograms does each friend get?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Split 7.2 into 6 + 1.2 — both parts divide nicely by 3.
    2. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 1.2 ÷ 3 = 0.4 (because 12 tenths ÷ 3 = 4 tenths).
    3. Put them back together: 2 + 0.4.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: each friend gets 2.4 kg. Check: 2.4 × 3 = 7.2 ✓

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a fraction?

    A fraction names equal parts of a whole. The bottom number — the denominator — tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number — the numerator — counts how many of those parts you take. So 3/4 means: cut into 4 equal parts, take 3 of them.

    2Equivalent fractions

    Equivalent fractions look different but show the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. The secret: multiply (or divide) both the numerator and the denominator by the same number and the value stays the same — you are only cutting smaller pieces, not changing the total amount. Dividing both by the same number is called simplifying.

    1/2 — multiply both by 2 →
    2/4 — multiply both by 2 →
    4/8 — simplify to go back

    3Comparing and ordering fractions

    Same denominator: just compare numerators — 5/8 > 3/8. Same numerator: careful, a bigger denominator means SMALLER pieces — 2/3 > 2/5! When both differ, convert to the same denominator (1/2 = 4/8 to compare with 5/8), or compare with the 1/2 benchmark: 3/8 is less than a half, while 5/8 is more than a half.

    4Fractions of amounts

    A fraction is also a “machine” that acts on numbers! To find 3/4 of 20: divide by the denominator (20 ÷ 4 = 5 — that is 1/4), then multiply by the numerator (5 × 3 = 15). Easy rule: “divide by the bottom, times by the top”.

    5Mixed numbers and improper fractions

    When the numerator is bigger than the denominator (like 7/4), the fraction is worth more than 1 — an improper fraction. We can rewrite it as a mixed number: 7/4 = 4/4 + 3/4 = 1¾. Seven quarter-slices = one whole pie and three slices left over.

    6Fractions ↔ decimals ↔ percentages

    Fractions, decimals and percentages are three “languages” for the same amount. A percentage is just a fraction out of 100: 1/2 = 50/100 = 50% = 0.5. Learn the key trios in the table below by heart — they appear everywhere!

    FractionDecimalPercentagePicture it
    1/20.550%Half the cake
    1/40.2525%A quarter — half of a half
    3/40.7575%Three quarters — nearly full
    1/100.110%One tenth
    3/50.660%3/5 = 6/10 — more than a half

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A class has 24 students. 3/4 of them love swimming. How many students love swimming?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Divide by the bottom: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 — each quarter is 6 students.
    2. Times by the top: 6 × 3 = 18.
    3. Sense check: 3/4 is most of the class, and 18 is indeed most of 24. ✓
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 18 students love swimming.
    Example 2

    Put these fractions in order from smallest to largest: 1/2, 3/8, 5/8.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Convert everything to eighths: 1/2 = 4/8.
    2. Now just compare numerators: 3/8, 4/8, 5/8.
    3. So the order is 3/8 < 1/2 < 5/8.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 — because 1/2 is really 4/8, sitting between 3/8 and 5/8.
    Example 3

    Write 3/5 as a decimal and as a percentage.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Make the denominator 10: multiply top and bottom by 2 → 3/5 = 6/10.
    2. 6/10 = 6 tenths = 0.6.
    3. Make the denominator 100: 6/10 = 60/100 = 60%.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%. Three ways of writing, one amount!

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a ratio?

    A ratio compares two amounts. The bead string below has 2 red beads and 3 blue beads — we write the ratio red : blue = 2:3, read as “for every 2 red beads there are 3 blue beads”. Order matters: 2:3 is not the same as 3:2!

    2Ratios and fractions — close cousins

    A ratio compares part with part; a fraction compares part with whole. With red:blue = 2:3, there are 2 + 3 = 5 parts in total — so 2/5 of the beads are red and 3/5 are blue. Add the sides of a ratio to find the total number of parts!

    Ratio (part : part)red : blue = 2 : 3 — comparing the two groups
    Fraction (part / whole)red = 2/5 of the whole string — comparing one group with everything

    3Simplifying and scaling ratios

    Like fractions, ratios can be multiplied or divided on both sides by the same number without changing their meaning. Divide both sides of 6:9 by 3 → 2:3 (simplest form). Multiply both sides of 1:2 by 4 → 4:8 (scaling up — used when multiplying recipes!).

    4Sharing in a ratio

    Share 20 sweets between An and Binh in the ratio 2:3. Three steps: ① Add the parts: 2 + 3 = 5 parts. ② Find one part: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 sweets. ③ Multiply up: An gets 2 × 4 = 8, Binh gets 3 × 4 = 12. Check: 8 + 12 = 20 ✓

    5Scaling recipes — ratios in the kitchen

    A lemonade recipe: 3 lemons make 6 glasses. Want 12 glasses (double)? Multiply both sides by 2: you need 6 lemons. Want just 2 glasses? Divide both sides by 3: you need 1 lemon. Keep the ratio the same and the taste never changes!

    Lemons 🍋Glasses 🥤How
    12divide both sides of 3:6 by 3
    36the original recipe
    612multiply both sides by 2
    918multiply both sides by 3

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A pencil case has 12 pencils and 8 pens. Write the ratio of pencils to pens in its simplest form.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Write the ratio in the order asked: 12 : 8.
    2. Find the biggest number that divides both sides — it is 4.
    3. Divide both sides by 4.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 12:8 = 3:2 — for every 3 pencils there are 2 pens.
    Example 2

    Two sisters share a $35 reward in the ratio 2:5 (the younger one did fewer chores!). How much does each sister get?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Add the parts: 2 + 5 = 7 parts.
    2. One part: $35 ÷ 7 = $5.
    3. Multiply up: 2 × $5 and 5 × $5.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: $10 and $25. Check: 10 + 25 = 35 ✓
    Example 3

    A recipe needs 2 cups of flour and 1 cup of sugar for 4 cupcakes. Nyna wants to bake 12 cupcakes. How much flour and sugar does she need?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. From 4 cupcakes to 12 is multiplying by 3.
    2. Multiply EVERY ingredient by 3 to keep the flour : sugar ratio at 2:1.
    3. Flour: 2 × 3; sugar: 1 × 3.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 6 cups of flour and 3 cups of sugar — the ratio is still 2:1, so the cupcakes taste exactly the same!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Reading an analogue clock

    The short hand shows the hour, the long hand shows the minutes. Each number on the face is worth 5 minutes for the long hand: the 1 = 5 minutes, the 5 = 25 minutes, the 6 = 30 minutes (half past). The clock below shows 7:25 — the short hand is just past the 7, and the long hand points at the 5 (25 minutes).

    2The 12-hour and 24-hour clock

    The 12-hour clock uses am (morning, before noon) and pm (afternoon and evening, after noon). The 24-hour clock counts straight from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59. Conversion rule: for pm times, add 12 — 3:40 pm = 15:40. Morning times stay the same — 9:15 am = 09:15.

    12-hour24-hourMoment of the day
    7:00 am07:00Getting up for school
    12:00 noon12:00Noon — the am/pm border
    3:40 pm15:40School ends (3:40 + 12)
    9:30 pm21:30Bedtime
    12:00 midnight00:00A new day begins

    3Reading timetables

    A timetable arranges times in a table. Read down a column to follow one bus; read along a row to watch one stop. Example: to reach the Pool before 15:30, check below — Bus 1 arrives 15:20 ✓, Bus 2 arrives 15:50 ✗ (too late).

    StopBus 1Bus 2Bus 3
    School14:4515:1515:45
    Library15:0015:3016:00
    Pool15:2015:5016:20

    Bus 1: leaves School 14:45, reaches the Pool 15:20 → a 35-minute journey.

    4Finding time intervals — the jump method

    To find how long it is from 09:45 to 11:20, do not subtract in columns! Jump along a time line: ① jump to the next whole hour (09:45 → 10:00 is 15 min), ② jump whole hours (10:00 → 11:00 is 1 hour), ③ jump the last bit (11:00 → 11:20 is 20 min). Total: 1 hour 35 minutes.

    5Seconds and stopwatches

    The time units: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day. For very short intervals, a stopwatch shows decimals of a second: 12.4 s means 12 seconds and 4 tenths of a second. In sport, 0.1 seconds can decide the gold medal!

    Run 1: 32.5 seconds
    Run 2: 31.9 seconds — faster!
    0.6 seconds quicker

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna's extra class starts at 3:40 in the afternoon. Write this time on the 24-hour clock.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Afternoon means pm — after noon.
    2. For pm times, add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15.
    3. The minutes stay the same: 40.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 15:40.
    Example 2

    A film starts at 10:35 and ends at 12:10. How long is the film?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Jump to the whole hour: 10:35 → 11:00 is 25 min.
    2. Jump one hour: 11:00 → 12:00 is 1 hour.
    3. Jump the rest: 12:00 → 12:10 is 10 min. Add all three jumps.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 25 min + 1 h + 10 min = 1 hour 35 minutes.
    Example 3

    Nyna swims 25 m in 58.3 seconds on Tuesday and 59.1 seconds on Thursday. Which day was faster, and by how much?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Faster = the SMALLER time: 58.3 < 59.1 → Tuesday was faster.
    2. Find the difference: count up from 58.3 → 59.1.
    3. 58.3 + 0.7 = 59.0, then 0.1 more = 59.1 → 0.8 seconds in total.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Tuesday was faster, by 0.8 seconds.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Types of triangle

    Triangles are named by their sides. Equilateral: 3 equal sides, all angles 60°. Isosceles: exactly 2 equal sides. Scalene: no equal sides at all. If a triangle has a 90° corner, we also call it right-angled. The little tick marks on the sides show which sides are equal.

    2Types of angle

    An angle measures the turn between two lines, in degrees (°). A full circle is 360°, a half turn (straight line) is 180°, and a quarter turn is a right angle, 90°. That gives the families: acute below 90°, right exactly 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, and reflex beyond 180°.

    Trick: compare every angle with the 90° book corner — smaller means acute, bigger means obtuse.

    3Perimeter — the distance around

    Perimeter is the total distance around the outside edge of a shape — like an ant walking around the rim. To find it: add up every side. For a rectangle with length l and width w: perimeter = l + w + l + w = 2 × (l + w).

    4Area — counting the squares inside

    Area is the space INSIDE a shape, measured in squares — cm² (square centimetres). For a rectangle, instead of counting every square, use the shortcut: area = length × width. The 5 × 3 rectangle below has 3 rows of 5 squares = 15 squares.

    Perimeter — plain unitsMeasures distance: cm, m, km. The ant walks AROUND the shape.
    Area — square unitsMeasures surface: cm², m². Paint covers INSIDE the shape.

    5Compound shapes — split them up

    A compound shape — like an L-shape — is built from rectangles joined together. To find its area: split it into rectangles, work each one out, then add. The L below = rectangle A (6 × 2) + rectangle B (3 × 2) = 12 + 6 = 18 squares.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What type of triangle is it?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Count the equal sides: 5 = 5, but 8 is different.
    2. Exactly 2 equal sides → check the triangle families.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: an isosceles triangle — because exactly two sides are equal.
    Example 2

    A rectangular playground is 7 m long and 4 m wide. Find its perimeter and its area.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Perimeter: add all four sides — 2 × (7 + 4).
    2. Area: length × width — 7 × 4.
    3. Mind the units: perimeter in m, area in m².
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: perimeter = 2 × 11 = 22 m; area = 7 × 4 = 28 m².
    Example 3

    An L-shape is built from: a 6 cm × 2 cm rectangle and a 3 cm × 2 cm rectangle. Find the total area.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Work out each rectangle: 6 × 2 = 12 and 3 × 2 = 6.
    2. Add the two areas together.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 12 + 6 = 18 cm². Splitting the compound shape into rectangles is the key!

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a line of symmetry? The fold test

    A line of symmetry splits a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other. The surest test: fold the shape along the line — if the two halves land exactly on top of each other, it really is a line of symmetry. You can also stand a small mirror on the line: if the shape still looks complete, the line is a mirror line!

    2Lines of symmetry in 2D shapes

    Each shape has its own number of symmetry lines. Square: 4 (2 middle lines + 2 diagonals). Rectangle: only 2 — its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry! Equilateral triangle: 3. Isosceles triangle: 1. Circle: infinitely many — every diameter is a mirror line. A lovely rule: a regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines.

    Careful with the rectangle: fold along a diagonal and the halves do NOT match!

    3Vertical and horizontal lines — and letters

    A line of symmetry can be vertical, horizontal or diagonal. The alphabet is a great playground: A, M, T, U, V have a vertical line; B, C, D, E, K have a horizontal one; H, I, O, X have both; and F, G, J, L have none at all!

    4Completing symmetrical patterns on a grid

    To complete a symmetrical pattern: for each shaded square, count how many squares it is from the mirror line, then shade the square the same distance on the other side, in the same row. In the grid below, the green squares reflect across the red line into the pale gold squares.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nam says: “A rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry, just like a square.” Is Nam right or wrong? Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Fold test on the two middle lines: the halves match ✓ — that is 2 lines.
    2. Now fold along a diagonal: one half sticks out, the halves do NOT match ✗.
    3. Diagonals only work when all sides are equal — that is, in a square.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Nam is wrong — a rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry (the two middle lines). The diagonals fail the fold test.
    Example 2

    On a grid, a square is shaded 2 squares to the left of the mirror line, in the third row. Where is its reflection?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. A reflection keeps the same ROW (the vertical position does not change).
    2. The distance to the mirror line stays the same — but on the other side.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 2 squares to the right of the mirror line, still in the third row.
    Example 3

    Which of the letters A, F, H, G, T have a vertical line of symmetry?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Imagine a vertical line down the middle of each letter.
    2. Is the left half a mirror of the right half? A ✓, T ✓, H ✓ (H even has a horizontal line too).
    3. F and G lean to one side — no symmetry lines at all.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: A, H and T have a vertical line of symmetry; F and G have none.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The coordinate grid: along the corridor, up the stairs

    The coordinate grid has two number lines: the x-axis running across and the y-axis running up, crossing at the origin (0,0). Every point has a coordinate pair (x, y). The magic phrase: “along the corridor, then up the stairs” — go ACROSS first (x), then UP (y). The point (3,2): 3 steps right, 2 steps up.

    2Order matters: (3,2) ≠ (2,3)

    A coordinate pair is an ordered pair: the first number is always x (across), the second always y (up). Swap them and you land on a completely different point! (3,2) sits low-right, while (2,3) sits high-left. Just like the address “house 3, floor 2” is not “house 2, floor 3”.

    3Shapes on grids — vertices

    Each corner of a shape is a vertex, named by its coordinates. Drawing a shape on a grid = plotting its vertices and joining them. A classic puzzle: given 3 vertices of a rectangle, find the 4th — use the parallel sides: the missing vertex “borrows” its x from one vertex and its y from another.

    4Translation — sliding shapes

    A translation slides a shape to a new place with no turning, no flipping, no resizing. The rule: add the same numbers to the x (right) and/or y (up) of EVERY vertex. Translating “3 right, 1 up”: (2,1) → (5,2).

    5Reflection on a grid

    Reflecting a shape in a mirror line on a grid: each vertex “jumps” to the other side, keeping its distance from the mirror line. Unlike a translation, the reflected image is flipped — like looking at yourself in a mirror. The size stays exactly the same.

    Translation — slideThe shape keeps facing the same way; every vertex makes the same journey.
    Reflection — flipThe shape flips over the mirror line; distances to the mirror stay equal.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    An wants to plot (1,4) but walks 4 steps right and then 1 step up. Which point did An actually plot, and how should (1,4) be plotted?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. 4 right then 1 up is the point (4,1) — the first number is always the ACROSS step.
    2. The real (1,4): 1 step right, then 4 steps up.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: An plotted (4,1). To plot (1,4): along the corridor 1, up the stairs 4.
    Example 2

    Three vertices of a rectangle are (1,1), (5,1) and (5,3). Find the fourth vertex.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Sketch the three points: (1,1) and (5,1) make the bottom edge; (5,3) is the top-right corner.
    2. The missing corner is top-left: directly above (1,1) → x = 1; level with (5,3) → y = 3.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1,3) — borrowing the x from (1,1) and the y from (5,3).
    Example 3

    The point (2,1) is translated 3 squares right and 1 square up. What are its new coordinates?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Right means adding to x: 2 + 3 = 5.
    2. Up means adding to y: 1 + 1 = 2.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (5,2). Right adds to x, up adds to y.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a Carroll diagram?

    A Carroll diagram is a 2×2 table that sorts things using two yes/no questions. For numbers: question 1 — “Is it even?” (rows); question 2 — “Is it greater than 10?” (columns). Every number answers both questions and lands in exactly one cell.

    2The “not” column — the other half of the world

    The secret of Carroll diagrams: each question splits the world into exactly two halves — “yes” and “not”. “Not even” is nothing mysterious — it is simply the odd numbers! Because of this clean split, NOTHING gets left out: everything belongs to one cell, and nothing belongs to two.

    Exactly one cell eachTwo answers (yes/no, yes/no) → exactly one of the 4 cells.
    “Not” = everything else“Not even” = odd; “not greater than 10” = 10 or less.

    3Reading a Carroll diagram

    A Carroll diagram is not just for sorting — it is for reading. “How many even numbers?” → add the whole “even” ROW. “How many are greater than 10?” → add that COLUMN. “How many are even AND greater than 10?” → just one single cell. All 4 cells together = the total number of items.

    QuestionWhere to lookExample (diagram in item 1)
    How many even?The whole “even” row3 + 2 = 5
    How many greater than 10?That whole column3 + 2 = 5
    Even AND greater than 10?One single cell3
    How many in total?All four cells3+2+2+3 = 10

    4Not just for numbers

    Carroll diagrams can sort anything, as long as the questions are yes/no: shapes (“has a right angle?” × “is a quadrilateral?”), animals (“can fly?” × “lays eggs?”), even your family (“wears glasses?” × “older than 12?”). Choosing good criteria is an art — each question must be so clear that every item has only one possible answer!

    2 yes/no questions
    4 cells — one home each
    Read and compare the groups

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A Carroll diagram has rows “even / not even” and columns “greater than 10 / not greater than 10”. Which cell does the number 7 belong to?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Question 1: is 7 even? No → the “not even” row.
    2. Question 2: is 7 greater than 10? No → the “not greater than 10” column.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the “not even, not greater than 10” cell — bottom right.
    Example 2

    In the diagram from theory item 1, how many of the numbers are odd?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Odd numbers = the “NOT even” row.
    2. Left cell: 11, 15 (2 numbers). Right cell: 3, 7, 9 (3 numbers).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 2 + 3 = 5 odd numbers — add the whole “not even” row.
    Example 3

    Shapes are sorted by “triangle / not triangle” and “has a right angle / no right angle”. Which cell does a SQUARE belong to?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Is a square a triangle? No — it has 4 sides → “not triangle”.
    2. Does a square have a right angle? Yes — all four corners! → “has a right angle”.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the “not triangle, has a right angle” cell.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Tally marks — the magic group of five

    Each tally is one upright stroke for ONE item. The fifth stroke does not stand upright — it crosses the first four, making a five-bar “gate”. So instead of counting stroke by stroke, you count gates in fives: 5, 10, 15… then add the leftover strokes.

    2Building a tally chart from a survey

    A tally chart has one row per choice. Surveying “What is your favourite fruit?”, you draw a stroke in the matching row the moment each person answers — nothing to remember! At the end, count each row's tallies and write them as the frequency column.

    FruitTallyFrequency
    Mango「「「「̸ 「「7
    Banana「「「「̸5
    Orange「「「3
    Total15

    Checking trick: the total frequency must equal the number of people asked!

    3Reading a tally chart

    From the chart above you can answer all kinds of questions: “Which fruit is most popular?” — mango (7). “How many more votes for mango than orange?” — 7 − 3 = 4. “How many children took part?” — add everything: 15. Read gates in fives — never count stroke by stroke!

    Most / fewestCompare row frequencies — the longest row wins.
    How many more?SUBTRACT one frequency from the other.
    TotalAdd every row's frequency.

    4Why tallies at all?

    Imagine counting cars passing the school gate: they whizz by non-stop, and you cannot keep writing “14, cross it out, 15…”. With tallies, each car costs just one pen stroke — nothing to erase, nothing to remember. Tallies are the perfect tool when data arrives live and fast: surveys, voting, keeping score in games.

    Event happens → 1 stroke
    Groups of 5 build up
    Count in 5s → frequency

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Draw the tally for the number 17.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Divide 17 by 5: 3 groups of five, remainder 2.
    2. Draw 3 complete gates (4 strokes + 1 diagonal each).
    3. Add 2 loose upright strokes.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 3 five-bar gates + 2 loose strokes (5 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 17).
    Example 2

    From the favourite-fruit chart (in the theory): how many more votes does mango have than banana?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Mango: 1 gate + 2 strokes = 7.
    2. Banana: 1 gate = 5.
    3. “How many more” = subtraction.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 7 − 5 = 2 votes.
    Example 3

    In a 10-minute traffic survey, Nyna tallies: motorbikes 4 gates + 3 strokes, cars 2 gates + 1 stroke. How many of each, and how many in total?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Motorbikes: 4 × 5 + 3 = 23.
    2. Cars: 2 × 5 + 1 = 11.
    3. Total: add the two counts.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 23 motorbikes, 11 cars — 34 vehicles in total.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a Venn diagram?

    A Venn diagram sorts with overlapping circles. Each circle has a rule. The region where the circles cross — the overlap — is for items that satisfy both rules. Below: multiples of 2 and multiples of 3 — the numbers 6 and 12 divide by both, so they stand right in the middle!

    2The four regions of a Venn diagram

    A two-circle Venn diagram has exactly 4 regions: ① left circle only, ② the intersection (both), ③ right circle only, ④ outside both circles (but still inside the box!). An item that fits neither rule is NOT thrown away — it stands outside the circles, inside the rectangle.

    ① Left only / ③ Right onlyPasses exactly one rule.
    ② The overlapPasses BOTH rules at once.
    ④ OutsidePasses neither — still part of the diagram!

    3Reading a Venn diagram

    Careful with counting questions! “How many numbers are in the ‘multiples of 2’ circle?” = left-only PLUS the overlap (the whole circle). “How many are ONLY multiples of 2?” = left-only alone. For the diagram in item 1: whole left circle = 4 + 2 = 6 numbers; left-only = 4.

    QuestionRegions to count
    In circle A?A-only + overlap
    ONLY in A?A-only (overlap not counted)
    In both A and B?The overlap only
    Total?All 4 regions, including outside

    4Venn and Carroll — two pictures, one story

    Venn and Carroll diagrams do the SAME job — sorting by two questions! Venn's four regions match Carroll's four cells exactly: the overlap = the “yes-yes” cell; outside = the “no-no” cell. Pick Venn when you want to SEE the sharing; pick Carroll when you want a tidy table for counting.

    Venn: overlapping circles
    Same data, same 4 groups
    Carroll: a 2×2 table

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    A Venn diagram has circles “multiples of 2” and “multiples of 3”. Where does the number 18 go?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. 18 ÷ 2 = 9 — divides exactly ✓ (a multiple of 2).
    2. 18 ÷ 3 = 6 — divides exactly ✓ (a multiple of 3).
    3. Both rules pass → which region?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the overlap — 18 is a multiple of both 2 and 3.
    Example 2

    A Venn diagram sorts animals by “can fly” and “can swim”. Place these animals: duck, eagle, dolphin, cat.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Duck: fly ✓ swim ✓ → the overlap.
    2. Eagle: fly ✓ swim ✗ → the “fly” circle only.
    3. Dolphin: fly ✗ swim ✓ → the “swim” circle only.
    4. Cat: ✗ ✗ → outside the circles.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: duck in the overlap; eagle fly-only; dolphin swim-only; cat outside both circles (but still inside the box!).
    Example 3

    A class has 25 children. The “football” circle holds 12 (including the overlap), the “badminton” circle holds 9 (including the overlap), and the overlap holds 4. How many children play neither sport?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Football-only: 12 − 4 = 8. Badminton-only: 9 − 4 = 5.
    2. Playing at least one sport: 8 + 4 + 5 = 17.
    3. Neither: 25 − 17.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 25 − 17 = 8 children play neither — they stand outside both circles. (Notice we did not count the 4 overlap children twice!)

    Practice

    Theory

    1From messy to a list

    Data usually arrives messy: “Lan 132cm, Minh 128cm, An 140cm, Hoa 135cm…”. Every statistician's first step is to organise it into an ordered list — alphabetical to find names fast, or by value to see instantly who is tallest. An ordered list makes searching child's play!

    Alphabetical orderAn, Hoa, Lan, Minh — look up any name in a flash.
    By value128, 132, 135, 140 — smallest and largest jump right out.

    2Tables: where rows meet columns

    A table is a list with superpowers: it arranges information in rows (across) and columns (down), with headings saying what each column means. To look something up: trace along its row, trace down its column — the answer waits at the crossing cell. Below: how many books did An read in February? Row “An” meets column “Feb” → 6.

    ReaderJanFebMarTotal
    An46515
    Bình33713
    Chi52613

    The “Total” column is a built-in check: 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 ✓

    3Two-way tables

    A two-way table categorises by TWO things at once — a close cousin of the Carroll diagram! The table below counts club choices by gender. Each cell answers a double question: “How many girls chose swimming?” → row “Girls” meets column “Swim” → 7. The “Total” row and column let you cross-check every number.

    SwimChessArtTotal
    Boys56314
    Girls74516
    Total1210830

    The bottom-right corner (30) must match both ways: 14+16 and 12+10+8 — a double check!

    4Building tables — and solving the blanks

    When building your own table, remember three things: ① clear headings for every column, ② include the units — “5” means nothing until you know it is 5 kg or 5 minutes!, ③ add a totals row if useful. And here is the detective trick: a blank cell in a table with totals can usually be worked out — the total minus the cells you know!

    Clear headings + units
    A totals row to check
    Blank cell? Total − known cells!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    From the reading table (theory item 2): who read the most books in March, and who leads overall?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. March: scan the “Mar” COLUMN — 5, 7, 6 → Bình is highest.
    2. Overall: scan the “Total” COLUMN — 15, 13, 13 → An leads.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: in March Bình read the most (7 books); overall An leads (15 books).
    Example 2

    In the two-way club table (item 3): how many children chose chess in total, and how many BOYS did not choose chess?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Chess total: the bottom of the “Chess” column — 10.
    2. Boys not choosing chess: boys' total (14) minus chess boys (6).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 10 children chose chess; 14 − 6 = 8 boys did not choose chess.
    Example 3

    A table row reads: Jan = 8, Feb = ?, Mar = 6, Total = 21. Find the blank cell.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The row must add up to 21.
    2. Known cells: 8 + 6 = 14.
    3. The blank = 21 − 14.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Feb = 21 − 14 = 7. Check: 8 + 7 + 6 = 21 ✓

    Practice

    Theory

    1Pictograms and the key

    A pictogram shows amounts with rows of repeated pictures. Its most important part is the key: it tells you how much EACH symbol is worth. The same row of 4 circles could mean 4 books (key ⚫ = 1) or 20 books (key ⚫ = 5) — skip the key and you are instantly wrong!

    Chi's row has a half symbol — half of 2 is 1, so Chi read 5 books.

    2Reading pictograms: multiply by the key

    The reading formula: number of symbols × key value = the real amount. A half symbol adds half the key. With key ⚫ = 10: three and a half symbols = 3 × 10 + 5 = 35. After reading, always ask: “Does this number make sense?”

    Whole symbolsMultiply by the key: 4 symbols × 2 = 8.
    Half symbolsAdd HALF the key: half of ⚫ = 10 is 5.

    3Drawing pictograms: choose the key wisely

    Drawing is the reverse: amount ÷ key = symbols to draw. Choose a key that keeps rows not too long, not too short: data 10, 20, 35 → key = 10 gives rows of 1, 2 and 3.5 symbols — neat! When the division gives a half (like 35 ÷ 10 = 3.5), draw a half symbol.

    Data: 10, 20, 35
    Pick key ⚫ = 10
    Draw 1, 2 and 3½ symbols

    4Comparing with pictograms

    A pictogram's power is comparing by eye: the longest row = the most popular category, instantly, no calculating. But for “how many more?”, convert to real numbers first and subtract — do not just count the extra symbols and forget to multiply by the key!

    Who wins? — just lookThe longest row is the champion (same key throughout).
    By how much? — must calculate2 extra symbols × key 5 = 10 more, not 2 more!

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    In the pictogram from item 1 (key ⚫ = 2 books): how many books did Bình read, and how many did all three children read together?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Bình: 3 symbols × 2 = 6 books.
    2. An: 4 × 2 = 8; Chi: 2.5 × 2 = 5.
    3. Total: 8 + 6 + 5.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: Bình read 6 books; all together they read 8 + 6 + 5 = 19 books.
    Example 2

    Class 4A scored 15 goals. With the key ⚽ = 5 goals, how many symbols should you draw? And with the key ⚽ = 2 goals?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Symbols = amount ÷ key.
    2. Key 5: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 whole symbols.
    3. Key 2: 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 → 7 symbols and a half.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: key 5 → 3 symbols; key 2 → 7 and a half symbols. Key 5 makes the tidier row!
    Example 3

    A pictogram (key ⭐ = 4 points): team Red has 6 symbols, team Blue has 4 and a half. How many points is Red ahead by?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Red: 6 × 4 = 24 points.
    2. Blue: 4 × 4 + 2 = 18 points (half symbol = 2).
    3. Difference: 24 − 18. (Do not answer “1.5 symbols”!)
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 24 − 18 = 6 points — that is 1.5 symbols × 4 points.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Block graphs and bar charts

    A block graph stacks each item as a tower of blocks; a bar chart is its grown-up version with solid bars. Bar height = amount. Always read the scale on the vertical axis first — each step might be worth 1, 2 or 10 units!

    2The mean — sharing out fairly

    The mean answers: “If everything were shared out equally, how much would each get?” The formula: add all the values, then divide by how many there are. For 3, 5, 7, 9: total = 24, four values → mean = 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Picture levelling the block towers until they are all the same height!

    3Mode and median

    The mode is the value appearing MOST OFTEN — the only average that works for words too (the class's most popular shirt colour!). The median: order the values smallest to largest and take the MIDDLE one. For 2, 3, 3, 5, 7: mode = 3 (appears twice), median = 3 (the third of five numbers).

    Mode — the repeat championThe most frequent value. Trick: MOde = MOst often.
    Median — the middle oneORDER first, then take the middle. A median strip runs down the middle of a road!

    4The range — how spread out?

    The range = biggest value MINUS smallest value. It is not an “average” — it measures how spread out the data is. Test scores 7, 8, 8, 9 have range 2 (very consistent); scores 2, 5, 8, 10 have range 8 (all over the place).

    Find highest and lowest
    Subtract: high − low
    Small range = consistent data

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nyna read 3, 5, 7 and 9 books over four months. What is her mean number of books per month?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Add: 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 24.
    2. Count: there are 4 values.
    3. Divide: 24 ÷ 4.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: mean = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 books per month.
    Example 2

    Five test scores: 7, 3, 9, 3, 8. Find the mode, the median and the range.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Order first: 3, 3, 7, 8, 9.
    2. Mode: which repeats? 3.
    3. Median: the middle (third of five) = 7.
    4. Range: 9 − 3 = 6.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: mode = 3, median = 7, range = 6. (Note: always order before finding the median!)
    Example 3

    From the goals bar chart (item 1): how many more goals did the Sharks score than the Pandas, and what is the mean goals per team?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Read the bars: Lions 6, Eagles 4, Sharks 8, Pandas 2.
    2. Difference: 8 − 2.
    3. Mean: (6+4+8+2) ÷ 4 = 20 ÷ 4.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the Sharks scored 6 more than the Pandas; the mean is 5 goals per team.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Number sequences and the step rule

    A sequence is numbers chained by a rule. To find the rule: work out the step between neighbouring terms. For 3, 7, 11, 15: every step is +4 — so the next term is 15 + 4 = 19. The rule must work at EVERY step, not just one!

    2Decreasing sequences — diving through zero

    Sequences can also decrease: 20, 17, 14, 11 has step −3. And remember unit 1.1: a falling sequence does not stop at zero! 5, 2, −1, −4… keeps subtracting 3, straight through 0 into negative numbers. Other rules exist too: 1, 2, 4, 8 doubles each step; 96, 48, 24 halves each step.

    Equal add / subtract3, 7, 11 (+4) · 20, 17, 14 (−3) — a constant step.
    Equal multiply / divide1, 2, 4, 8 (×2) · 96, 48, 24 (÷2) — the jumps themselves grow or shrink.

    3Shape patterns: repeating and growing

    A repeating pattern loops one block: 🔴🔵🔵|🔴🔵🔵|… — the block has period 3. To know position 10: count 10 around the loop of 3 → 10 = 3+3+3+1 → same as position 1 → 🔴. A growing pattern adds pieces at each figure — count the pieces of the first few figures and find the number rule!

    4Testing the rule and predicting far ahead

    The 3-step detective routine: ① work out ALL the steps, ② state the rule (“add 5” / “double”), ③ predict by applying the rule onward. Beware the trap: 1, 2, 4… might be “doubling” (next: 8) or “add 1, add 2, add 3” (next: 7) — you need more terms to be sure!

    ① Find every step
    ② State the rule
    ③ Predict and check

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Find the rule and the next TWO terms of: 6, 13, 20, 27…

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The steps: 13−6 = 7; 20−13 = 7; 27−20 = 7 — “add 7” works at every step.
    2. Next: 27 + 7 = 34, then 34 + 7 = 41.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the rule is “add 7”; the next two terms are 34 and 41.
    Example 2

    Continue 10, 7, 4, 1… for two more terms. What special thing happens?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The step: −3 each time.
    2. 1 − 3 = −2 — the sequence dives through zero!
    3. −2 − 3 = −5.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: −2 and −5 — the sequence passes straight through zero into negatives, just like unit 1.1 taught us!
    Example 3

    A bracelet repeats the block 🔴🔵🔵 (red, blue, blue). What colour is the 11th bead?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The period is 3 beads.
    2. 11 = 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 — three full loops with 2 left over.
    3. Position 2 of the block 🔴🔵🔵 is… blue.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: blue — bead 11 matches position 2 of the repeating block.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The five words of chance

    Probability measures how likely an event is to happen. We place every event on a scale from impossible — it can never happen — through unlikely, even chance and likely, up to certain — it will definitely happen.

    2Count outcomes to judge the chance

    How to judge a chance: count the outcomes. A spinner with 4 sectors — 3 green, 1 red: green is likely (3 out of 4), red is unlikely (1 out of 4). A coin has 2 equal faces: heads is an even chance. On a 1–6 dice: rolling a 7 is impossible, rolling less than 7 is certain!

    More winning outcomes → likely3 green marbles in a bag of 4: picking green is likely.
    Few winning outcomes → unlikely1 red marble in a bag of 4: picking red is unlikely — but not impossible!

    3Fair or unfair?

    A game is fair when every outcome has an equal chance. A spinner cut into 4 equal sectors is fair; a spinner where one sector is three times bigger is unfair. A balanced coin is fair — that is why football matches use one for kick-off!

    4Talk like a forecaster

    Probability language is everywhere: the weather forecast says a “70% chance of rain” (likely — pack an umbrella!), commentators say a team is “almost certain to win”. A subtle point: unlikely does not mean never — unlikely things still happen! And chance has no memory: three heads in a row does not make tails more likely next time.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    For a normal 1–6 dice, pick the right word for each event: (a) rolling an 8; (b) rolling an even number; (c) rolling a number less than 7.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. (a) The faces only show 1–6 — there is no 8.
    2. (b) Even numbers: 2, 4, 6 — exactly 3 of the 6 outcomes.
    3. (c) Every face 1–6 is less than 7.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) impossible; (b) even chance (3 out of 6 = half); (c) certain.
    Example 2

    A bag holds 7 strawberry sweets and 1 lemon sweet. Nyna picks one with her eyes closed. Which probability word fits “picking strawberry”? Is it certain?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. 7 of the 8 outcomes are strawberry — most, but not all.
    2. There is still 1 path to the lemon sweet, so we cannot say “certain”.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: likely (very likely, even) — but NOT certain, because the lemon sweet could still be picked.
    Example 3

    Two friends play with a half-and-half spinner: green half — An wins, red half — Binh wins. Then they switch to a spinner where green fills ¾. Which game is fair? Why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. The half-and-half spinner: two equal halves → both players have an equal chance.
    2. The ¾-green spinner: An wins far more easily — the chances are no longer equal.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the first game is fair (an even chance each); the second is unfair because the sectors are not equal.

    Practice

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Negative number
    Số âm

    Negative numbers are numbers less than 0, written with a minus sign in front, like −3.

    Negative numbers (Số âm) là các số nhỏ hơn 0, được viết với dấu trừ ở phía trước, ví dụ −3.

    Place value
    Giá trị theo hàng

    Every digit sits in a place, and that place tells you the digit's value.

    Mỗi chữ số đứng ở một hàng, và hàng đó cho biết giá trị của chữ số (Place value — Giá trị theo hàng).

    Digit
    Chữ số

    In 45 672, the digit 4 is in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 40 000.

    Trong số 45 672, Digit (Chữ số) 4 đứng ở hàng chục nghìn, nên có giá trị 40 000.

    Number line
    Trục số

    On the number line, negative numbers sit to the left of zero.

    Trên Number line (Trục số), số âm nằm ở bên trái số 0.

    Zero
    Số không

    When you count back, do not stop at zero — keep going into the negative numbers.

    Khi đếm lùi, đừng dừng lại ở Zero (Số không) — hãy đi tiếp sang các số âm.

    Compare
    So sánh

    We compare two numbers with the symbols >, < and =.

    Chúng ta Compare (So sánh) hai số bằng các ký hiệu >, < và =.

    Ascending order
    Thứ tự tăng dần

    Ascending order means smallest to largest.

    Ascending order (Thứ tự tăng dần) nghĩa là xếp từ nhỏ nhất đến lớn nhất.

    Descending order
    Thứ tự giảm dần

    Descending order means largest to smallest.

    Descending order (Thứ tự giảm dần) nghĩa là xếp từ lớn nhất đến nhỏ nhất.

    Round
    Làm tròn

    To round a number means to snap it to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand.

    Round (Làm tròn) một số nghĩa là đưa nó về số tròn chục, tròn trăm hoặc tròn nghìn gần nhất.

    Temperature
    Nhiệt độ

    At night in Sa Pa, the temperature is −6°C — six degrees below zero.

    Ban đêm ở Sa Pa, Temperature (Nhiệt độ) là −6°C — sáu độ dưới 0.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Decimal
    Số thập phân

    A decimal number uses a decimal point to show parts smaller than one whole.

    Decimal (Số thập phân) dùng dấu phẩy thập phân để thể hiện các phần nhỏ hơn một đơn vị.

    Decimal point
    Dấu phẩy thập phân

    The decimal point separates the whole part from the parts smaller than one.

    Decimal point (Dấu phẩy thập phân) ngăn cách phần nguyên với phần nhỏ hơn một.

    Tenth
    Phần mười

    The first digit after the decimal point counts the tenths — in 3.47 there are 4 tenths.

    Chữ số đầu tiên sau dấu phẩy đếm các Tenth (Phần mười) — trong 3.47 có 4 phần mười.

    Hundredth
    Phần trăm (1/100)

    The second digit after the decimal point counts the hundredths — in 3.47 there are 7 hundredths.

    Chữ số thứ hai sau dấu phẩy đếm các Hundredth (Phần trăm) — trong 3.47 có 7 phần trăm.

    Whole number
    Số tự nhiên

    A whole number has no fraction part — like 3, 47 or 1 000.

    Whole number (Số tự nhiên) không có phần thập phân — như 3, 47 hay 1 000.

    Add
    Cộng

    To add decimals, line up the decimal points first.

    Muốn Add (Cộng) các số thập phân, trước hết phải đặt các dấu phẩy thẳng hàng.

    Subtract
    Trừ

    When you subtract 1.8 from 5, write 5 as 5.0 first.

    Khi Subtract (Trừ) 1.8 khỏi 5, hãy viết 5 thành 5.0 trước.

    Multiply
    Nhân

    To multiply a decimal by 10, every digit slides one place to the left.

    Khi Multiply (Nhân) một số thập phân với 10, mọi chữ số trượt sang trái một hàng.

    Divide
    Chia

    To divide by 10, every digit slides one place to the right — 74 ÷ 10 = 7.4.

    Khi Divide (Chia) cho 10, mọi chữ số trượt sang phải một hàng — 74 ÷ 10 = 7.4.

    Estimate
    Ước lượng

    Estimate first: 4.83 + 2.9 is close to 5 + 3, so the answer should be near 8.

    Hãy Estimate (Ước lượng) trước: 4.83 + 2.9 gần bằng 5 + 3, nên đáp án phải ở gần 8.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Fraction
    Phân số

    A fraction names equal parts of a whole — like 3/4 of a pizza.

    Fraction (Phân số) gọi tên các phần bằng nhau của một tổng thể — như 3/4 chiếc pizza.

    Numerator
    Tử số

    The numerator is the top number — it counts how many parts you have.

    Numerator (Tử số) là số ở trên — nó đếm xem con có bao nhiêu phần.

    Denominator
    Mẫu số

    The denominator is the bottom number — it tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into.

    Denominator (Mẫu số) là số ở dưới — cho biết tổng thể được cắt thành bao nhiêu phần bằng nhau.

    Equivalent fraction
    Phân số bằng nhau

    1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 are equivalent fractions — same amount, different names.

    1/2, 2/4 và 4/8 là các Equivalent fraction (Phân số bằng nhau) — cùng một lượng, khác tên gọi.

    Simplify
    Rút gọn

    To simplify 2/8, divide top and bottom by 2 to get 1/4.

    Muốn Simplify (Rút gọn) 2/8, chia cả tử và mẫu cho 2 để được 1/4.

    Mixed number
    Hỗn số

    1¾ is a mixed number — a whole number and a fraction together.

    1¾ là một Mixed number (Hỗn số) — một số nguyên đi cùng một phân số.

    Improper fraction
    Phân số có tử lớn hơn mẫu

    7/4 is an improper fraction — the top is bigger than the bottom, so it is worth more than 1.

    7/4 là một Improper fraction (Phân số có tử lớn hơn mẫu) — tử lớn hơn mẫu, nên nó lớn hơn 1.

    Percentage
    Phần trăm (%)

    A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — so 1/2 = 50/100 = 50%.

    Percentage (Phần trăm) là phân số trên 100 — nên 1/2 = 50/100 = 50%.

    Half
    Một nửa

    A half (1/2) is one of two equal parts — and half of a half is a quarter.

    Half (Một nửa, 1/2) là một trong hai phần bằng nhau — và một nửa của một nửa là một phần tư.

    Quarter
    Một phần tư

    A quarter (1/4) is one of four equal parts: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

    Quarter (Một phần tư, 1/4) là một trong bốn phần bằng nhau: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Ratio
    Tỉ số

    A ratio like 2:3 compares two amounts — 2 parts of one thing for every 3 parts of another.

    Ratio (Tỉ số) như 2:3 so sánh hai lượng — cứ 2 phần thứ này thì có 3 phần thứ kia.

    Proportion
    Tỉ lệ

    Two ratios that are equal are in proportion — 1:2 and 3:6 are in proportion.

    Hai tỉ số bằng nhau thì cùng Proportion (Tỉ lệ) — 1:2 và 3:6 cùng tỉ lệ.

    Part
    Phần

    In the ratio 2:3 there are 5 parts in total — 2 parts and 3 parts.

    Trong tỉ số 2:3 có tổng cộng 5 Part (Phần) — 2 phần và 3 phần.

    Whole
    Tổng thể

    Add the parts of a ratio to find the whole: 2 + 3 = 5 parts.

    Cộng các phần của tỉ số để được Whole (Tổng thể): 2 + 3 = 5 phần.

    Simplest form
    Dạng tối giản

    6:9 in its simplest form is 2:3 — divide both sides by 3.

    6:9 ở Simplest form (Dạng tối giản) là 2:3 — chia cả hai vế cho 3.

    Share
    Chia phần

    To share 20 sweets in the ratio 2:3, first work out the size of one part.

    Muốn Share (Chia phần) 20 viên kẹo theo tỉ số 2:3, trước hết tính xem một phần bằng bao nhiêu.

    Scale up
    Nhân rộng

    Multiply both sides of a ratio by the same number to scale it up: 1:2 → 4:8.

    Nhân cả hai vế của tỉ số với cùng một số để Scale up (Nhân rộng): 1:2 → 4:8.

    For every
    Cứ mỗi

    The ratio 2:3 says: for every 2 red beads there are 3 blue beads.

    Tỉ số 2:3 nói rằng: For every (Cứ mỗi) 2 hạt đỏ thì có 3 hạt xanh.

    Double
    Gấp đôi

    To make a recipe for twice as many people, double every ingredient.

    Muốn nấu cho số người gấp đôi, hãy Double (Gấp đôi) mọi nguyên liệu.

    Recipe
    Công thức nấu ăn

    A recipe is a real-life ratio: 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of sugar.

    Recipe (Công thức nấu ăn) chính là tỉ số ngoài đời: cứ 2 cốc bột thì 1 cốc đường.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Analogue clock
    Đồng hồ kim

    An analogue clock shows the time with a short hour hand and a long minute hand.

    Analogue clock (Đồng hồ kim) chỉ giờ bằng kim giờ ngắn và kim phút dài.

    Digital clock
    Đồng hồ số

    A digital clock shows the time with numbers, like 15:40.

    Digital clock (Đồng hồ số) hiển thị giờ bằng các con số, như 15:40.

    24-hour clock
    Đồng hồ 24 giờ

    The 24-hour clock counts straight from 00:00 to 23:59 — 3:40 pm becomes 15:40.

    24-hour clock (Đồng hồ 24 giờ) đếm thẳng từ 00:00 đến 23:59 — 3:40 chiều thành 15:40.

    Timetable
    Thời gian biểu

    A timetable lists times in a table — like when each bus leaves and arrives.

    Timetable (Thời gian biểu) liệt kê các mốc giờ trong bảng — như giờ mỗi chuyến xe buýt đi và đến.

    Interval
    Khoảng thời gian

    The interval from 09:45 to 11:20 is 1 hour 35 minutes.

    Interval (Khoảng thời gian) từ 09:45 đến 11:20 là 1 giờ 35 phút.

    Duration
    Thời lượng

    The duration of the film is 1 hour 35 minutes.

    Duration (Thời lượng) của bộ phim là 1 giờ 35 phút.

    Noon
    Giữa trưa

    Noon is 12:00 in the middle of the day — after it, times become pm.

    Noon (Giữa trưa) là 12:00 giữa ngày — sau đó, giờ chuyển sang pm.

    Midnight
    Nửa đêm

    Midnight is 00:00 — the moment a new day begins.

    Midnight (Nửa đêm) là 00:00 — thời khắc một ngày mới bắt đầu.

    Stopwatch
    Đồng hồ bấm giờ

    A stopwatch measures short times exactly, like 12.4 seconds — decimals of a second!

    Stopwatch (Đồng hồ bấm giờ) đo các khoảng ngắn thật chính xác, như 12.4 giây — số thập phân của giây!

    Second
    Giây

    There are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour.

    Có 60 Second (Giây) trong một phút và 60 phút trong một giờ.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Triangle
    Hình tam giác

    A triangle has 3 sides, 3 corners and 3 angles that always add up to 180°.

    Triangle (Hình tam giác) có 3 cạnh, 3 đỉnh và 3 góc luôn cộng lại bằng 180°.

    Angle
    Góc

    An angle measures the amount of turn between two lines, in degrees.

    Angle (Góc) đo độ mở giữa hai đường thẳng, tính bằng độ.

    Acute angle
    Góc nhọn

    An acute angle is smaller than 90° — sharp like a slice of cake.

    Acute angle (Góc nhọn) nhỏ hơn 90° — nhọn như một miếng bánh.

    Obtuse angle
    Góc tù

    An obtuse angle is bigger than 90° but smaller than 180° — a wide open door.

    Obtuse angle (Góc tù) lớn hơn 90° nhưng nhỏ hơn 180° — như cánh cửa mở rộng.

    Right angle
    Góc vuông

    A right angle is exactly 90° — the corner of every book and door.

    Right angle (Góc vuông) đúng bằng 90° — góc của mọi cuốn sách và cánh cửa.

    Equilateral
    (Tam giác) đều

    An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles of 60°.

    Tam giác Equilateral (đều) có 3 cạnh bằng nhau và 3 góc bằng nhau, mỗi góc 60°.

    Isosceles
    (Tam giác) cân

    An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and 2 equal base angles.

    Tam giác Isosceles (cân) có 2 cạnh bằng nhau và 2 góc ở đáy bằng nhau.

    Perimeter
    Chu vi

    The perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape — add up every side.

    Perimeter (Chu vi) là quãng đường vòng quanh hình — cộng tất cả các cạnh.

    Area
    Diện tích

    Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units like cm².

    Area (Diện tích) là phần không gian bên trong hình, đo bằng đơn vị vuông như cm².

    Compound shape
    Hình ghép

    A compound shape is made of simple shapes joined together — split it up to find its area.

    Compound shape (Hình ghép) được tạo từ các hình đơn giản ghép lại — hãy tách ra để tính diện tích.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Symmetry
    Tính đối xứng

    A shape has symmetry when one half is the mirror image of the other.

    Một hình có Symmetry (Tính đối xứng) khi một nửa là ảnh gương của nửa kia.

    Line of symmetry
    Trục đối xứng

    A square has 4 lines of symmetry; a rectangle has only 2.

    Hình vuông có 4 Line of symmetry (Trục đối xứng); hình chữ nhật chỉ có 2.

    Mirror line
    Đường gương

    Place a mirror on the mirror line and the shape looks complete again.

    Đặt một chiếc gương lên Mirror line (Đường gương) và hình sẽ trông nguyên vẹn trở lại.

    Reflection
    Ảnh phản chiếu

    The reflection of a point sits the same distance on the other side of the mirror line.

    Reflection (Ảnh phản chiếu) của một điểm nằm cách đường gương một khoảng bằng vậy ở phía bên kia.

    Symmetrical
    Có tính đối xứng

    A butterfly is symmetrical — fold it down the middle and the wings match.

    Con bướm Symmetrical (Có tính đối xứng) — gấp dọc chính giữa thì hai cánh khớp nhau.

    Fold
    Gấp

    The fold test: fold along the line — if the halves match exactly, it is a line of symmetry.

    Phép thử gấp: Fold (Gấp) theo đường kẻ — nếu hai nửa khớp hoàn toàn, đó là trục đối xứng.

    Pattern
    Hoạ tiết

    To complete a symmetrical pattern, reflect every shaded square across the mirror line.

    Muốn hoàn thành Pattern (Hoạ tiết) đối xứng, hãy phản chiếu từng ô tô màu qua đường gương.

    Regular polygon
    Đa giác đều

    A regular polygon with n equal sides has exactly n lines of symmetry.

    Regular polygon (Đa giác đều) có n cạnh bằng nhau thì có đúng n trục đối xứng.

    Vertical
    Thẳng đứng

    The letter A has a vertical line of symmetry, running from top to bottom.

    Chữ A có trục đối xứng Vertical (Thẳng đứng), chạy từ trên xuống dưới.

    Horizontal
    Nằm ngang

    The letter B has a horizontal line of symmetry, running from left to right.

    Chữ B có trục đối xứng Horizontal (Nằm ngang), chạy từ trái sang phải.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Coordinates
    Toạ độ

    Coordinates like (4,2) name an exact point: 4 across, then 2 up.

    Coordinates (Toạ độ) như (4,2) gọi tên chính xác một điểm: 4 sang ngang, rồi 2 lên trên.

    Grid
    Lưới ô vuông

    A coordinate grid is a field of squares with two numbered axes.

    Grid (Lưới ô vuông) toạ độ là một vùng ô vuông với hai trục được đánh số.

    Axis
    Trục

    The two number lines of a grid are called axes — one across, one up.

    Hai trục số của lưới được gọi là Axis (Trục) — một nằm ngang, một thẳng đứng.

    X-axis
    Trục hoành (x)

    The x-axis runs ACROSS — the first coordinate counts along it.

    X-axis (Trục hoành) chạy NGANG — toạ độ thứ nhất đếm dọc theo nó.

    Y-axis
    Trục tung (y)

    The y-axis runs UP — the second coordinate climbs it.

    Y-axis (Trục tung) chạy DỌC — toạ độ thứ hai leo lên theo nó.

    Origin
    Gốc toạ độ

    The origin (0,0) is where the two axes cross — every journey starts there.

    Origin (Gốc toạ độ) (0,0) là nơi hai trục cắt nhau — mọi hành trình bắt đầu từ đó.

    Plot
    Vẽ điểm

    To plot (4,2): slide 4 along the x-axis, then climb 2 up, and mark the point.

    Để Plot (Vẽ điểm) (4,2): trượt 4 theo trục x, rồi leo 2 lên trên, và đánh dấu điểm.

    Vertex
    Đỉnh

    Each corner of a shape is a vertex — a rectangle has four vertices.

    Mỗi góc của hình là một Vertex (Đỉnh) — hình chữ nhật có bốn đỉnh.

    Translation
    Phép tịnh tiến

    A translation slides a shape across the grid without turning or flipping it.

    Translation (Phép tịnh tiến) trượt hình trên lưới mà không xoay hay lật nó.

    Position
    Vị trí

    Coordinates describe position exactly — no more "over there somewhere"!

    Toạ độ mô tả Position (Vị trí) một cách chính xác — không còn kiểu "ở đâu đó đằng kia"!

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Carroll diagram
    Sơ đồ Carroll

    A Carroll diagram sorts things into a 2×2 table using yes/no questions.

    Carroll diagram (Sơ đồ Carroll) phân loại mọi thứ vào bảng 2×2 bằng các câu hỏi có/không.

    Sort
    Phân loại

    To sort numbers, ask each one the two questions and place it in the matching cell.

    Để Sort (Phân loại) các số, hỏi mỗi số hai câu hỏi và đặt nó vào ô phù hợp.

    Criterion
    Tiêu chí

    "Is it even?" is a criterion — a yes/no question used for sorting.

    "Nó có chẵn không?" là một Criterion (Tiêu chí) — câu hỏi có/không dùng để phân loại.

    Cell
    Ô

    A Carroll diagram with two criteria has exactly 4 cells.

    Sơ đồ Carroll với hai tiêu chí có đúng 4 Cell (Ô).

    Row
    Hàng

    The rows answer the first question: even on the top row, not even below.

    Các Row (Hàng) trả lời câu hỏi thứ nhất: chẵn ở hàng trên, không chẵn ở hàng dưới.

    Column
    Cột

    The columns answer the second question: greater than 10, or not.

    Các Column (Cột) trả lời câu hỏi thứ hai: lớn hơn 10, hay không.

    Even
    Số chẵn

    Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 — they split into two equal teams.

    Even (Số chẵn) tận cùng bằng 0, 2, 4, 6 hoặc 8 — chúng chia được thành hai đội bằng nhau.

    Odd
    Số lẻ

    Odd numbers — 1, 3, 5, 7, 9… — always leave one left over when paired.

    Odd (Số lẻ) — 1, 3, 5, 7, 9… — luôn dư ra một khi ghép cặp.

    Property
    Tính chất

    Shapes can be sorted by their properties: number of sides, right angles, symmetry.

    Các hình có thể được phân loại theo Property (Tính chất): số cạnh, góc vuông, tính đối xứng.

    Data
    Dữ liệu

    The numbers, shapes or facts you sort are your data.

    Các con số, hình hoặc thông tin con phân loại chính là Data (Dữ liệu).

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Tally
    Vạch đếm

    A tally is a quick stroke you draw each time you count one more item.

    Tally (Vạch đếm) là nét vạch nhanh con vẽ mỗi lần đếm thêm một mục.

    Tally chart
    Bảng vạch đếm

    A tally chart records counts with tally marks while a survey happens.

    Tally chart (Bảng vạch đếm) ghi số đếm bằng vạch ngay trong lúc khảo sát.

    Frequency
    Tần số

    The frequency of mango is 7 — seven people chose it.

    Frequency (Tần số) của xoài là 7 — bảy người đã chọn nó.

    Survey
    Khảo sát

    In our class survey, everyone named their favourite fruit.

    Trong Survey (Khảo sát) của lớp, mỗi bạn nêu tên loại quả yêu thích.

    Count
    Đếm

    Count completed tally groups in fives: 5, 10, 15…

    Count (Đếm) các nhóm vạch hoàn chỉnh theo năm: 5, 10, 15…

    Total
    Tổng

    Add every row's frequency to find the total number of answers.

    Cộng tần số của mọi hàng để ra Total (Tổng) số câu trả lời.

    Record
    Ghi lại

    Record each answer the moment you hear it — one stroke at a time.

    Record (Ghi lại) từng câu trả lời ngay khi nghe thấy — mỗi lần một vạch.

    Group of five
    Nhóm năm

    The fifth tally crosses the first four, making a neat group of five.

    Vạch thứ năm gạch chéo qua bốn vạch đầu, tạo thành Group of five (Nhóm năm) gọn gàng.

    Stroke
    Nét vạch

    Each stroke stands for exactly one item counted.

    Mỗi Stroke (Nét vạch) đại diện cho đúng một mục được đếm.

    Result
    Kết quả

    Turn the tallies into numbers to read the survey's results.

    Đổi các vạch thành con số để đọc Result (Kết quả) của khảo sát.

    Venn diagram
    Sơ đồ Venn

    A Venn diagram sorts things into overlapping circles.

    Venn diagram (Sơ đồ Venn) phân loại mọi thứ vào các vòng tròn chồng lên nhau.

    Overlap
    Phần chồng nhau

    The overlap is the football-shaped region where the two circles cross.

    Overlap (Phần chồng nhau) là vùng hình quả bóng bầu dục nơi hai vòng tròn cắt nhau.

    Intersection
    Phần giao

    Items in the intersection belong to BOTH groups at once.

    Các mục trong Intersection (Phần giao) thuộc về CẢ HAI nhóm cùng lúc.

    Set
    Tập hợp

    Each circle holds one set — like the set of multiples of 2.

    Mỗi vòng tròn chứa một Set (Tập hợp) — như tập hợp các bội số của 2.

    Belong
    Thuộc về

    Ask of every item: which circle (or circles) does it belong to?

    Hỏi với từng mục: nó Belong (Thuộc về) vòng tròn nào (hay cả hai)?

    Circle
    Vòng tròn

    Each circle is labelled with its rule, like "can fly".

    Mỗi Circle (Vòng tròn) được dán nhãn quy tắc của nó, như "biết bay".

    Both
    Cả hai

    A duck can fly AND swim — it satisfies both rules, so it sits in the overlap.

    Vịt vừa bay VỪA bơi được — thoả mãn Both (Cả hai) quy tắc, nên nằm ở phần chồng nhau.

    Neither
    Không cái nào

    Items that fit neither circle sit outside the circles, inside the box.

    Các mục Neither (Không thuộc cái nào) nằm ngoài các vòng tròn, bên trong khung.

    Multiple
    Bội số

    6 is a multiple of both 2 and 3 — so it lives in the overlap.

    6 là Multiple (Bội số) của cả 2 và 3 — nên nó sống ở phần chồng nhau.

    Group
    Nhóm

    Venn diagrams show how two groups share some members.

    Sơ đồ Venn cho thấy hai Group (Nhóm) chia sẻ một số thành viên như thế nào.

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    List
    Danh sách

    A list puts items one under another — a sorted list is even quicker to search.

    List (Danh sách) xếp các mục nối tiếp nhau — danh sách đã sắp xếp còn tra nhanh hơn.

    Table
    Bảng

    A table organises information into rows and columns.

    Table (Bảng) tổ chức thông tin thành các hàng và cột.

    Heading
    Tiêu đề cột

    The headings tell you what each column of the table shows.

    Heading (Tiêu đề cột) cho biết mỗi cột của bảng thể hiện điều gì.

    Two-way table
    Bảng hai chiều

    A two-way table sorts data by two things at once — like sport and gender.

    Two-way table (Bảng hai chiều) phân loại dữ liệu theo hai yếu tố cùng lúc — như môn thể thao và giới tính.

    Look up
    Tra cứu

    To look up a value, find where its row meets its column.

    Muốn Look up (Tra cứu) một giá trị, tìm nơi hàng của nó gặp cột của nó.

    Information
    Thông tin

    Tables pack a lot of information into a small, tidy space.

    Bảng gói được rất nhiều Information (Thông tin) vào một không gian nhỏ gọn.

    Organise
    Tổ chức, sắp xếp

    Organise messy data into a table and patterns appear like magic.

    Organise (Sắp xếp) dữ liệu lộn xộn vào bảng và các quy luật hiện ra như phép màu.

    Units
    Đơn vị

    Good tables name their units: kg, cm, đồng — otherwise 5 could mean anything!

    Bảng tốt luôn ghi rõ Units (Đơn vị): kg, cm, đồng — nếu không, số 5 có thể là bất cứ gì!

    Entry
    Mục nhập

    Each number written in a table is one entry.

    Mỗi con số ghi trong bảng là một Entry (Mục nhập).

    Blank
    Ô trống

    A blank cell in a totals table can often be worked out from the other entries.

    Blank (Ô trống) trong bảng có hàng tổng thường có thể suy ra từ các mục khác.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Pictogram
    Biểu đồ tranh

    A pictogram shows amounts using rows of little pictures.

    Pictogram (Biểu đồ tranh) thể hiện số lượng bằng các hàng hình vẽ nhỏ.

    Symbol
    Ký hiệu

    Each symbol in a pictogram stands for the same amount.

    Mỗi Symbol (Ký hiệu) trong biểu đồ tranh đại diện cho cùng một lượng.

    Key
    Chú giải

    The key says what one symbol is worth — for example, ⚫ = 2 books.

    Key (Chú giải) cho biết một ký hiệu đáng giá bao nhiêu — ví dụ ⚫ = 2 cuốn sách.

    Half symbol
    Nửa ký hiệu

    A half symbol shows half the key's value — half of ⚫ = 2 is 1.

    Half symbol (Nửa ký hiệu) thể hiện một nửa giá trị chú giải — nửa của ⚫ = 2 là 1.

    Represent
    Đại diện

    In this pictogram, one apple symbol represents 5 real apples.

    Trong biểu đồ tranh này, một ký hiệu quả táo Represent (Đại diện) cho 5 quả táo thật.

    Amount
    Số lượng

    Multiply symbols by the key to find the real amount.

    Nhân số ký hiệu với chú giải để ra Amount (Số lượng) thật.

    Category
    Hạng mục

    Each row of a pictogram is one category — one flavour, one sport, one class.

    Mỗi hàng của biểu đồ tranh là một Category (Hạng mục) — một vị kem, một môn thể thao, một lớp.

    Scale
    Tỉ lệ

    A scaled pictogram uses a key bigger than 1 — like one symbol for every 10 votes.

    Biểu đồ tranh có Scale (Tỉ lệ) dùng chú giải lớn hơn 1 — như một ký hiệu cho mỗi 10 phiếu.

    Popular
    Phổ biến

    The most popular choice owns the longest row of symbols.

    Lựa chọn Popular (Phổ biến) nhất sở hữu hàng ký hiệu dài nhất.

    Chart
    Biểu đồ

    Pictograms, bar charts and tables are all charts — pictures of data.

    Biểu đồ tranh, biểu đồ cột và bảng đều là Chart (Biểu đồ) — những bức tranh của dữ liệu.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Block graph
    Biểu đồ khối

    A block graph shows each amount as a tower of blocks or a bar.

    Block graph (Biểu đồ khối) thể hiện mỗi lượng bằng một tháp khối hoặc một cột.

    Bar
    Cột

    The tallest bar belongs to the biggest amount.

    Bar (Cột) cao nhất thuộc về lượng lớn nhất.

    Average
    Số trung bình

    An average sums up a whole data set with one typical number.

    Average (Số trung bình) tóm tắt cả bộ dữ liệu bằng một con số tiêu biểu.

    Mean
    Trung bình cộng

    Mean = add all the values, then divide by how many there are.

    Mean (Trung bình cộng) = cộng tất cả giá trị, rồi chia cho số lượng giá trị.

    Mode
    Mốt

    The mode is the value that appears most often.

    Mode (Mốt) là giá trị xuất hiện thường xuyên nhất.

    Median
    Trung vị

    Order the values, and the median is the one sitting exactly in the middle.

    Sắp xếp các giá trị, Median (Trung vị) là giá trị ngồi đúng chính giữa.

    Range
    Khoảng biến thiên

    Range = biggest value minus smallest value — how spread out the data is.

    Range (Khoảng biến thiên) = giá trị lớn nhất trừ nhỏ nhất — dữ liệu trải rộng cỡ nào.

    Value
    Giá trị

    Each number in your data set is one value.

    Mỗi con số trong bộ dữ liệu là một Value (Giá trị).

    Highest
    Cao nhất

    The highest value tops the range calculation.

    Giá trị Highest (Cao nhất) đứng đầu phép tính khoảng biến thiên.

    Lowest
    Thấp nhất

    Range = highest − lowest.

    Khoảng biến thiên = cao nhất − Lowest (thấp nhất).

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Sequence
    Dãy số

    A sequence is a list of numbers following a rule: 3, 7, 11, 15…

    Sequence (Dãy số) là danh sách các số tuân theo một quy tắc: 3, 7, 11, 15…

    Term
    Số hạng

    Each number in a sequence is called a term — 11 is the third term of 3, 7, 11…

    Mỗi số trong dãy được gọi là Term (Số hạng) — 11 là số hạng thứ ba của 3, 7, 11…

    Rule
    Quy tắc

    The rule tells you how to get from one term to the next — like "add 4".

    Rule (Quy tắc) cho biết cách đi từ số hạng này sang số hạng kế — như "cộng 4".

    Increase
    Tăng

    2, 4, 6, 8 is an increasing sequence — each term is bigger.

    2, 4, 6, 8 là dãy Increase (Tăng) — mỗi số hạng lớn dần.

    Decrease
    Giảm

    20, 17, 14, 11 is a decreasing sequence — it can even dive past zero!

    20, 17, 14, 11 là dãy Decrease (Giảm) — nó thậm chí có thể lặn qua số 0!

    Repeat
    Lặp lại

    A repeating pattern loops the same block again and again: 🔴🔵🔵 🔴🔵🔵…

    Hoạ tiết Repeat (Lặp lại) quay vòng cùng một khối mãi: 🔴🔵🔵 🔴🔵🔵…

    Predict
    Dự đoán

    Once you know the rule, you can predict terms far ahead.

    Khi đã biết quy tắc, con có thể Predict (Dự đoán) các số hạng ở xa phía trước.

    Next
    Kế tiếp

    Apply the rule to the last term to find the next one.

    Áp dụng quy tắc vào số hạng cuối để tìm số Next (Kế tiếp).

    Step
    Bước nhảy

    The step of 3, 7, 11 is +4 — the same jump every time.

    Step (Bước nhảy) của 3, 7, 11 là +4 — cú nhảy giống nhau mỗi lần.

    Growing pattern
    Hoạ tiết lớn dần

    In a growing pattern, each figure gains more pieces than the one before.

    Trong Growing pattern (Hoạ tiết lớn dần), mỗi hình nhận thêm nhiều mảnh hơn hình trước.

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Probability
    Xác suất

    Probability measures how likely something is to happen, from impossible to certain.

    Probability (Xác suất) đo mức độ một điều có khả năng xảy ra, từ không thể tới chắc chắn.

    Certain
    Chắc chắn

    It is certain that the sun will rise tomorrow morning.

    Certain (Chắc chắn) là mặt trời sẽ mọc vào sáng mai.

    Impossible
    Không thể

    Rolling a 7 on a normal 1–6 dice is impossible.

    Impossible (Không thể) là gieo được số 7 trên xúc xắc thường 1–6.

    Likely
    Có khả năng cao

    If 9 of 10 marbles are green, picking green is likely.

    Nếu 9 trong 10 viên bi màu xanh, bốc được bi xanh là Likely (Có khả năng cao).

    Unlikely
    Khó xảy ra

    Snow in Hanoi is very unlikely — but not impossible!

    Tuyết rơi ở Hà Nội là Unlikely (Khó xảy ra) — nhưng không phải là không thể!

    Even chance
    Cơ hội ngang nhau

    A coin flip gives an even chance of heads or tails — perfectly balanced.

    Tung đồng xu cho Even chance (Cơ hội ngang nhau) giữa sấp và ngửa — cân bằng hoàn hảo.

    Outcome
    Kết quả

    A dice roll has six possible outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

    Một lần gieo xúc xắc có sáu Outcome (Kết quả) có thể: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 và 6.

    Event
    Sự kiện

    "Rolling an even number" is an event made of the outcomes 2, 4 and 6.

    "Gieo được số chẵn" là một Event (Sự kiện) gồm các kết quả 2, 4 và 6.

    Fair
    Công bằng

    A fair spinner gives every sector the same chance.

    Vòng quay Fair (Công bằng) cho mọi ô cùng một cơ hội như nhau.

    Chance
    Cơ hội

    The weather report says there is a small chance of rain today.

    Bản tin thời tiết nói hôm nay có Chance (Cơ hội) mưa nhỏ.
