    Did you know?

    • Ancient Chinese mathematicians used negative numbers more than 2,000 years ago — they calculated with counting rods, using red rods for positive numbers and black rods for negative ones.Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics ↗
    • In the year 628, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta was the first to write down rules for calculating with negative numbers — he called positive numbers “fortunes” and negative numbers “debts”.Source: Encyclopædia Britannica ↗
    • The coldest temperature ever measured on Earth is −89.2°C, at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983 — about 70 degrees colder than your freezer at home!Source: Encyclopædia Britannica ↗
    • The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest land on Earth — about 430 metres BELOW sea level. On maps, its elevation is written as a negative number: about −430 m.Source: Encyclopædia Britannica ↗
    • The deepest point in the ocean — the Challenger Deep in the Pacific — sits at about −10,935 metres. If you dropped Mount Everest in, its peak would still be more than 2 km underwater!Source: NOAA Ocean Service ↗

    Negative numbers in real life

    Freezer

    About −18°C — cold enough to keep ice cream frozen

    Lift buttons

    Basement floors B1, B2 are floors −1, −2 — below ground level

    Scuba diver

    Diving 10 m down means being at −10 m compared with the sea surface

    Money

    If you owe 5,000 đồng, your balance is −5,000 đồng

    Golf scores

    In golf, a score of −3 (3 under par) is a GOOD score — the lower the negative, the better!

    Weather forecast

    In winter at Sa Pa or Mẫu Sơn, the temperature can drop to −2°C, with frost and snow

    Glossary

    Negative number
    A number less than 0, written with a minus sign in front, like −3.
    Place value
    The value of a digit based on its place — in 45 672, the digit 4 is worth 40 000.
    Digit
    One of the ten symbols 0–9 used to write every number.
    Number line
    A straight line with numbers spaced evenly along it — negatives left of zero, positives right.
    Zero
    The boundary between positive and negative numbers — neither positive nor negative itself.
    Compare
    Deciding which number is bigger, smaller or equal, using the symbols >, <, =.
    Ascending order
    Smallest to largest — like walking up a staircase.
    Descending order
    Largest to smallest — like walking down a staircase.
    Round
    Snapping a number to the nearest ten / hundred / thousand. Digit 5 or more → go up.
    Temperature
    How hot or cold something is — the easiest place to meet negative numbers in real life (below 0°C).

    Try it yourself: go on a negative-number hunt around your home! Check the freezer temperature, the lift buttons at the shopping centre, and open a weather app to see Sa Pa's temperature in winter. How many negative numbers can you find in one day?

    Did you know?

    • Decimal fractions as we write them today were made popular in Europe by Simon Stevin in 1585, in a little book called 'De Thiende' — 'The Tenth'.Source: Britannica ↗
    • NASA engineers only need about 15 decimal places of pi to steer spacecraft across the whole Solar System with amazing accuracy.Source: NASA JPL ↗

    Decimals in real life

    Price tags

    $3.45 means 3 dollars and 45 hundredths of a dollar (45 cents)

    Race times

    Sprinters are separated by hundredths of a second — 10.49 s beats 10.61 s

    Body temperature

    A thermometer reads 37.5°C — the .5 is five tenths of a degree

    Market scales

    1.25 kg of mangoes = 1 whole kilogram and 25 hundredths more

    Heights

    Your height 1.38 m sits between 1 m and 2 m on a decimal number line

    Glossary

    Decimal
    A number with a whole part and a fraction part, separated by a point — like 3.47.
    Decimal point
    The dot in a decimal number — everything to its right is smaller than one whole.
    Tenth
    One whole split into 10 equal parts — 1/10 = 0.1.
    Hundredth
    One whole split into 100 equal parts — 1/100 = 0.01.
    Whole number
    A number with nothing after the decimal point: 0, 1, 2, 3…
    Add
    Putting numbers together to find the total.
    Subtract
    Taking one number away from another to find the difference.
    Multiply
    Adding the same number again and again — 2.4 × 3 means 2.4 + 2.4 + 2.4.
    Divide
    Sharing a number into equal parts.
    Estimate
    A sensible rough answer you work out before calculating exactly.

    Try it yourself: next time you go shopping, read three price tags out loud as decimals, and work out in your head what two of them cost together. Check with a calculator — how close was your estimate?

    Did you know?

    • Over 3,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians wrote almost all fractions as sums of unit fractions with 1 on top, like 1/2 + 1/4 — as shown on the famous Rhind Mathematical Papyrus.Source: British Museum ↗
    • The Rhind papyrus, an Egyptian maths 'textbook' from around 1650 BC, contains fraction tables and 84 maths problems for students — homework from 3,600 years ago!Source: Britannica ↗

    Fractions in real life

    Pizza slices

    A pizza cut into 8 slices — eat 3 and you have eaten 3/8 of it

    Half-time

    Half-time in football is exactly 1/2 of the match played

    Sale signs

    "50% off" means the price drops by one half

    Recipes

    Recipes use fractions all the time: 1/2 cup of sugar, 1/4 spoon of salt

    Fuel gauge

    The fuel gauge shows the tank as fractions: full, 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, empty

    Glossary

    Fraction
    A number that names equal parts of a whole, written one number over another.
    Numerator
    The top number of a fraction — how many parts are taken.
    Denominator
    The bottom number of a fraction — how many equal parts the whole is split into.
    Equivalent fraction
    Fractions that look different but show exactly the same amount.
    Simplify
    Making a fraction as simple as possible by dividing top and bottom by the same number.
    Mixed number
    A whole number and a fraction written together, like 1¾.
    Improper fraction
    A fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom number — worth more than one whole.
    Percentage
    A special fraction out of 100, written with the % sign.
    Half
    One of two equal parts: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.
    Quarter
    One of four equal parts: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

    Try it yourself: at your next family meal, be the fraction reporter! What fraction of the pizza has been eaten? What fraction of the water bottle is left? Can you spot two fractions that are secretly equivalent?

    Did you know?

    • The golden ratio, about 1.618, is a special ratio people have claimed to spot everywhere from the ancient Greek Parthenon to famous paintings and seashells.Source: Britannica ↗
    • Sunflower seeds grow in spirals whose counts are neighbouring Fibonacci numbers (like 34 and 55) — and dividing one by the other gets closer and closer to the golden ratio.Source: National Museum of Mathematics ↗

    Ratios in real life

    Cooking rice

    Rice to water is about 1:1.5 — the ratio that makes perfect rice

    Mixing paint

    3 parts blue + 1 part white makes the same light blue every time

    Maps

    A 1:100 000 map means 1 cm on paper is 100 000 cm (1 km) in real life

    Squash & water

    Mix syrup and water 1:4 — too little water and it is too sweet!

    Screens

    A TV screen ratio of 16:9 means 16 units wide for every 9 units tall

    Glossary

    Ratio
    A comparison of two amounts, written with a colon — like 2:3.
    Proportion
    When two ratios are equal — the amounts grow or shrink together fairly.
    Part
    One equal share used to build a ratio.
    Whole
    Everything together — all the parts of the ratio added up.
    Simplest form
    A ratio written with the smallest possible whole numbers.
    Share
    Splitting an amount into groups that follow a ratio.
    Scale up
    Making both sides of a ratio bigger by multiplying them by the same number.
    For every
    The phrase that unlocks ratios: "for every X of these, Y of those".
    Double
    Multiplying by 2 — the simplest way to scale a ratio up.
    Recipe
    Cooking instructions built on ratios of ingredients.

    Try it yourself: help cook dinner tonight and hunt for the ratios — rice to water, noodles to broth, syrup to water. If you doubled the meal for guests, what would each ingredient become?

    Did you know?

    • We have 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in a minute because the ancient Babylonians did their maths in a number system based on 60.Source: Scientific American ↗
    • A day on Mars, called a 'sol', lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes — just a little longer than a day on Earth.Source: Royal Museums Greenwich ↗

    School timetable

    Lessons, breaks and lunch all follow a timetable of start and end times

    Airport boards

    Departure boards use the 24-hour clock: flight VN216 departs 17:45

    Sports timing

    Races are timed to hundredths of a second with a stopwatch

    Cooking timers

    Boil the egg 7 minutes, bake the cake 35 minutes — cooking is full of durations

    Sunrise & sunset

    Weather apps list sunrise 05:52 and sunset 18:20 — a day length puzzle!

    Glossary

    Analogue clock
    A clock with moving hands on a round face.
    Digital clock
    A clock that shows the time as numbers instead of hands.
    24-hour clock
    Time written from 00:00 to 23:59 with no am or pm needed.
    Timetable
    A table of times showing when things happen — buses, trains, lessons.
    Interval
    The gap between two times.
    Duration
    How long something lasts from start to finish.
    Noon
    12 o'clock in the middle of the day.
    Midnight
    12 o'clock at night — written 00:00 on the 24-hour clock.
    Stopwatch
    A timer for measuring exactly how long something takes.
    Second
    A small unit of time — 60 of them make one minute.

    Did you know?

    • The triangle is the strongest shape in engineering — that is why you see triangles everywhere in bridges and towers.Source: Let's Talk Science ↗
    • Bees build their honeycomb in hexagons because that shape holds the most honey while using the least wax.Source: PBS NOVA ↗

    Shapes and measures in real life

    Fencing a garden

    How much fence to buy? That is the perimeter of the garden

    Floor tiles

    How many tiles cover the floor? That is the area in squares

    Bridges & roofs

    Triangles make bridges and roofs strong and stable

    Pizza slices

    Each slice makes an angle at the centre — 8 equal slices = 45° each

    Clock hands

    At 3:00 the hands make a perfect right angle — 90°

    Glossary

    Triangle
    A shape with exactly three straight sides.
    Angle
    The amount of turn between two lines that meet, measured in degrees (°).
    Acute angle
    An angle smaller than 90°.
    Obtuse angle
    An angle between 90° and 180°.
    Right angle
    An angle of exactly 90°, marked with a small square.
    Equilateral
    A triangle with all three sides (and angles) equal.
    Isosceles
    A triangle with exactly two equal sides.
    Perimeter
    The total distance around the outside of a shape.
    Area
    The amount of space inside a shape, counted in squares (cm²).
    Compound shape
    A shape built from two or more simple shapes, like an L made of two rectangles.

    Try it yourself: go on a right-angle hunt around your home — book corners, door frames, tables. Then estimate the perimeter of your bedroom in footsteps, and check by walking it!

    Did you know?

    • A butterfly's wings are almost perfectly symmetrical — the pattern on one wing is a mirror image of the other.Source: Super Simple ↗
    • Snowflakes grow with six symmetrical arms because of how frozen water molecules line up — and no two snowflakes are exactly alike.Source: NOAA ↗

    Symmetry in real life

    Butterflies & faces

    Wings and faces mirror down the middle — nature loves symmetry

    Buildings

    Temples, palaces and bridges are often perfectly symmetrical

    Letters & logos

    A, H, M, O, T have vertical mirror lines — many logos use symmetry too

    Paper snowflakes

    Fold paper, snip, unfold — the cuts repeat symmetrically!

    Mirrors at home

    Stand a small mirror on a picture to complete it symmetrically

    Glossary

    Symmetry
    When one half of a shape mirrors the other half exactly.
    Line of symmetry
    A fold line that splits a shape into two matching mirror halves.
    Mirror line
    Another name for the line of symmetry — where a mirror would stand.
    Reflection
    The flipped image of a shape on the other side of the mirror line.
    Symmetrical
    Describing a shape that has at least one line of symmetry.
    Fold
    Bending a shape along a line to see if the halves match.
    Pattern
    A design of shapes or colours — symmetrical when both sides mirror.
    Regular polygon
    A shape whose sides and angles are all equal — its symmetry lines equal its sides.
    Vertical
    Standing straight up and down, like a flagpole.
    Horizontal
    Lying flat from left to right, like the horizon.

    Try it yourself: make a paper snowflake — fold a square of paper twice, snip little shapes from the edges, then unfold. Count how many lines of symmetry your snowflake has!

    Did you know?

    • Legend says René Descartes invented coordinates while lying in bed watching a fly on the ceiling, wondering how to describe exactly where it was.Source: Wild Maths (Cambridge) ↗
    • Sailors and pilots use a giant coordinate grid drawn over the whole Earth — latitude and longitude — to find any place on the planet.Source: Britannica Kids ↗

    Coordinates in real life

    Chess

    Every chess square has a name like e4 — a letter across, a number up

    Battleship

    Call "B7!" — the classic game is pure coordinate practice

    Maps & GPS

    GPS pins your position with two numbers: latitude and longitude

    Cinema seats

    Row F, seat 12 — your ticket is a coordinate pair!

    Treasure maps

    "4 paces east, 2 paces north" — pirates translated before mathematicians did

    Glossary

    Coordinates
    A pair of numbers (x,y) that names an exact point on a grid.
    Grid
    The square field where points are plotted.
    Axis
    One of the two number lines that frame the grid.
    X-axis
    The horizontal axis — walk along it first.
    Y-axis
    The vertical axis — climb it second.
    Origin
    The corner point (0,0) where the axes meet.
    Plot
    To mark a point on the grid at its coordinates.
    Vertex
    A corner point of a shape, named by its coordinates.
    Translation
    Sliding a shape to a new position — same size, same way up.
    Position
    Where something is — pinned down exactly by coordinates.

    Try it yourself: draw a 6×6 grid, hide three "treasures" at secret coordinates, and let someone find them by calling coordinate pairs — battleship style. Whoever needs fewer guesses wins!

    Did you know?

    • Carroll diagrams are named after Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland — his real name was Charles Dodgson, and he taught mathematics at Oxford.Source: Wikipedia ↗
    • In 1886 Lewis Carroll invented a board game called The Game of Logic, played with counters on diagrams, to teach children how to reason logically.Source: Lehigh University Libraries ↗

    Carroll-style sorting in real life

    Sorting laundry

    Whites / colours × delicate / normal — a Carroll diagram in the laundry basket

    Lunch menu

    Vegetarian / not × spicy / mild — restaurants sort dishes with two questions

    Toy tidy-up

    Soft / hard × big / small — four boxes and every toy has exactly one home

    Library shelves

    Fiction / non-fiction × for kids / for adults — books sort into four sections

    Animal groups

    Can fly / cannot × lays eggs / does not — scientists sort creatures this way

    Glossary

    Carroll diagram
    A 2×2 sorting table based on yes/no questions, named after Lewis Carroll.
    Sort
    Putting things into groups by their properties.
    Criterion
    A yes/no test used to decide where something belongs.
    Cell
    One box of the table — every item lands in exactly one cell.
    Row
    A line of cells running across the table.
    Column
    A line of cells running down the table.
    Even
    A number that divides exactly by 2.
    Odd
    A number that leaves 1 left over when divided by 2 — the "not even" family.
    Property
    A feature something has — used as a sorting question.
    Data
    The collection of facts or things being sorted and studied.

    Try it yourself: draw a 2×2 Carroll diagram and sort your family: "wears glasses / doesn't" across the top, "older than 12 / not" down the side. Which cell is fullest?

    Glossary

    Tally
    A counting stroke — one mark for one item.
    Tally chart
    A table that collects counts using tally marks.
    Frequency
    How many times something happens or is chosen.
    Survey
    Asking a group of people questions to collect data.
    Count
    Finding how many — tallies make counting fast.
    Total
    Everything added together.
    Record
    Writing information down as it happens.
    Group of five
    Four strokes plus a diagonal fifth — the tally "gate".
    Stroke
    One single tally line.
    Result
    What the data shows once it is counted up.

    Try it yourself: run a 5-minute traffic survey from your window — tally motorbikes, cars and trucks in separate rows. Which vehicle wins? Could you have kept up writing full numbers instead?

    Did you know?

    • Venn diagrams are named after English mathematician John Venn, who introduced them in 1880 as a way of picturing sets.Source: Britannica ↗
    • A stained-glass window at Gonville and Caius College in Cambridge shows a colourful Venn diagram, honouring John Venn who studied and taught there.Source: Linda Hall Library ↗

    Venn diagrams in real life

    Two sports teams

    Some children play football, some play badminton — a few play both!

    Music playlists

    Songs you like, songs your friend likes — the overlap is your shared playlist

    Food sorting

    Sweet things, healthy things — fruit lands happily in the overlap

    Animal skills

    Can fly / can swim — ducks and swans rule the overlap

    Choosing a film

    Films Mum likes ∩ films you like = tonight's movie

    Glossary

    Venn diagram
    Overlapping circles that sort items into groups, named after John Venn.
    Overlap
    The middle region shared by both circles.
    Intersection
    The maths name for the overlap — where both tests are passed.
    Set
    A collection of things that share a property.
    Belong
    To be a member of a group.
    Circle
    One labelled ring of the Venn diagram.
    Both
    Passing the two tests at the same time.
    Neither
    Failing both tests — outside the circles but still in the diagram.
    Multiple
    A number in a times table: multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9, 12…
    Group
    A collection of items sorted together.

    Try it yourself: draw two overlapping circles labelled "likes durian" and "likes coffee", then place everyone in your family. Who ends up in the overlap — and who sits outside both circles?

    Did you know?

    • People were organising maths into tables 3,700 years ago — the Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322 is a table of numbers pressed into clay.Source: Wikipedia ↗
    • In 1839 George Bradshaw printed the world's first book of railway timetables, so travellers could look up train times in neat tables.Source: History of Information ↗

    Lists and tables in real life

    Menus

    Dish names in one column, prices in the next — a menu is a table

    League tables

    Football standings: teams, wins, losses, points — all in rows and columns

    TV guide

    Channels down the side, times across the top — find your show at the crossing

    Shopping receipts

    Item, quantity, price — and the total row at the bottom must add up!

    Calendars

    A calendar is a table: weeks are rows, weekdays are columns

    Glossary

    List
    Items written one after another, often in a helpful order.
    Table
    Information arranged in rows and columns.
    Heading
    The label at the top of a column (or start of a row).
    Two-way table
    A table that categorises by rows AND columns at the same time.
    Look up
    Finding one exact piece of information in a table.
    Information
    Facts and figures that tell you something.
    Organise
    Arranging things tidily so they are easy to use.
    Units
    What the numbers measure — kg, cm, minutes, đồng.
    Entry
    One piece of data written into a cell.
    Blank
    An empty cell — sometimes a puzzle you can solve!

    Did you know?

    • The Olympic Games have used sport pictograms since Tokyo 1964, when Japanese designers drew little picture symbols so visitors from any country could find their way without words.Source: Olympics.com ↗
    • The world's first writing — Sumerian cuneiform, over 5,000 years old — began as pictographs: small pictures standing for real things, just like pictogram symbols.Source: Britannica ↗

    Pictograms in real life

    Weather apps

    Sun, cloud and rain icons are pictograms telling the forecast at a glance

    Olympic signs

    Each sport has its own little figure — swimming, archery, football

    Map legends

    A tree = forest, a tent = campsite — map keys are pictogram keys

    Star ratings

    ★★★★½ — apps and films measured in symbols, halves included!

    Airport icons

    Suitcase, taxi, toilets — pictures guide travellers of every language

    Glossary

    Pictogram
    A chart that uses repeated pictures to show amounts.
    Symbol
    One little picture in the pictogram.
    Key
    The note telling you how much each symbol stands for.
    Half symbol
    Half a picture, worth half of whatever the key says.
    Represent
    To stand for something else.
    Amount
    How much or how many of something there is.
    Category
    One group being counted — one row of the chart.
    Scale
    Using one symbol to stand for several items instead of just one.
    Popular
    Chosen or liked by the most people.
    Chart
    Any picture that displays data clearly.

    Try it yourself: track the fruit your family eats for one week, then draw a pictogram with 1 symbol = 2 fruits. Do you need any half symbols? Which fruit wins the longest row?

    Did you know?

    • The bar chart was invented around 1786 by a Scotsman called William Playfair — who also invented the line graph and the pie chart!Source: Wikipedia ↗
    • Nurse Florence Nightingale used colourful 'rose' charts of hospital data to convince the British government to make hospitals cleaner and save soldiers' lives.Source: Science Museum Group ↗

    Averages in real life

    Sports statistics

    A striker's goals-per-season average tells you how good they really are

    Weather reports

    "Average temperature 28°C" sums up a whole month in one number

    Test scores

    The class mean shows how the whole class performed

    Growth charts

    Doctors compare your height with the average for your age

    Screen time

    Your tablet reports "daily average: 1 h 20 min" — that is a mean!

    Glossary

    Block graph
    A chart where bar heights show amounts.
    Bar
    One rectangle of the graph — taller means more.
    Average
    One number that describes the middle of a data set — mean, mode and median are all averages.
    Mean
    The share-out-equally average: total ÷ count.
    Mode
    The most common value — works for words too!
    Median
    The middle value of an ORDERED list.
    Range
    Biggest minus smallest — the spread of the data.
    Value
    One piece of numerical data.
    Highest
    The biggest value in the data.
    Lowest
    The smallest value in the data.

    Try it yourself: measure everyone in your family with a tape measure, then find the mean, the median, and the range of the heights. Is anyone exactly average?

    Did you know?

    • The spirals of seeds in a sunflower head almost always come in Fibonacci numbers like 34, 55 or 89 — a number pattern growing right in the garden.Source: Science (AAAS) ↗
    • Pinecones, pineapples and many seashells also grow following the Fibonacci pattern, where each number is the sum of the two before it.Source: Mathnasium ↗

    Patterns in real life

    Music beats

    Drum rhythms repeat in loops — boom-tap-tap, boom-tap-tap

    Calendars

    Mon…Sun then back to Mon — a repeating pattern with period 7

    Floor tiles

    Bathroom tiles repeat their design in perfect grids

    House numbers

    One side of the street counts 1, 3, 5… the other 2, 4, 6…

    The seasons

    Spring, summer, autumn, winter — nature's repeating pattern

    Glossary

    Sequence
    Numbers arranged one after another by a rule.
    Term
    One member of a sequence.
    Rule
    The instruction that generates the sequence.
    Increase
    Getting bigger from term to term.
    Decrease
    Getting smaller from term to term.
    Repeat
    Playing the same block of a pattern over and over.
    Predict
    Working out what comes next before seeing it.
    Next
    The term right after the current one.
    Step
    The gap between neighbouring terms.
    Growing pattern
    A shape pattern that adds pieces at every stage.

    Try it yourself: hunt for three patterns at home — in tiles, fences, songs or house numbers. For each one, say the rule out loud and predict what comes next. Were you right?

    Did you know?

    • Probability theory was born in 1654, when mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters about how to split the prize of an unfinished dice game fairly.Source: American Physical Society ↗
    • When the forecast says "30% chance of rain", it means that on 100 days exactly like today, about 30 of them would bring rain.Source: Royal Meteorological Society ↗

    Probability in real life

    Weather forecasts

    "70% chance of rain" — probability decides if you pack an umbrella

    Board games

    Dice and spinners run on chance — that's what makes games exciting

    Sports

    Commentators say a team is "likely to win" — probability talk!

    Coin toss kick-off

    Football matches start with a fair 50–50 coin flip

    Lucky draws

    Raffles at school fairs — more tickets means a bigger chance

    Glossary

    Probability
    How likely an event is to happen.
    Certain
    Definitely going to happen — probability 1.
    Impossible
    Can never happen — probability 0.
    Likely
    Will probably happen, but not for sure.
    Unlikely
    Will probably not happen, but still could.
    Even chance
    Equally likely to happen or not happen.
    Outcome
    One possible result of an experiment.
    Event
    Something that may or may not happen.
    Fair
    Every outcome has an equal chance.
    Chance
    Another everyday word for probability.

    Try it yourself: flip a coin 20 times and tally heads and tails. Before you start, predict the result. Was it exactly 10–10? Close? Talk about why chance doesn't always match the prediction exactly.

    Backup to a file & restore

    Cách hoạt động · How it works

    Desktop Chrome/Edge: on the first Save, pick the folder containing this HTML file — every Save then writes the .json (named after this file + date-time) straight there, and each time the page opens it auto-loads the newest one (if the browser re-asks permission, tap the yellow bar). Phones/other browsers: the file downloads to Downloads; load it back with the yellow button.

    🌐 Get backup online (Google Drive or public GitHub)

    Thiết lập một lần (chỉ phụ huynh) · One-time setup (parent only)

    A public GitHub repo needs NOTHING extra — just paste the repo link (github.com/user/repo or …/tree/branch/folder). Google Drive only: browsers block webpages from reading Drive directly (CORS), so an API key is needed — create it free ONCE at console.cloud.google.com (project → enable the Google Drive API → Credentials → API key, with NO referrer restriction). It can only read public files. Share the Drive folder as "Anyone with the link — Viewer". Paste the key below — it is remembered and included in backups, so the child and other devices never need to touch this section.
